note: First Article Inspection records (item 47). An FAI verifies EVERY claim an artefact's own header makes, exhaustively, before the artefact is trusted -- a different question from the adversarial review, which asks whether a hostile reader can find a bug. The claim-to-arm mapping in each record was made BY READING. It is not generated and must not be: word-overlap scoring of prose claims against prose arm labels returned 38% with five false positives out of five on this platform (2026-09-14). tools/first_article_check.py verifies that a mapping exists, disposes of every claim, and still describes the bytes on disk -- not that the arm somebody named tests the claim they named it for.
required_from_note: Forward only, and the date is the day AFTER the requirement was written on purpose. 22 tools were first committed on 2026-09-15 by four sessions working in parallel; none of them could have followed a rule that did not exist yet, and reporting them as findings would make the gate's first run a wall of noise about work nobody did wrong. A rule starts when it is announced. The tools that pre-date it are uninspected and that debt is real -- the COUNT is printed on every run rather than written here, because a count in prose goes stale the first week and nothing makes it fail. tools/entity_baseline_readiness.py pre-dates the requirement too and is inspected anyway: it is the first article.

inspections.author_note: SELF-INSPECTION, AND IT IS THE WEAKEST KIND OF EVIDENCE IN THIS FILE. I wrote the tool and the control in the same sitting, so the claim-to-arm mapping is the author reading his own header -- exactly the blind spot the independent-review rule exists for. It is recorded because the gate names any artefact first committed on or after the requirement date and leaving it uninspected is worse. It should be re-read by another session, and the concurrency arms in particular deserve a second pair of eyes: a control written by the person who chose the design is the least likely place for that design to be doubted.

claims.claim: REPORT ONLY: it reads the registry and this session's own section, and the ONLY thing it ever writes is that one section.
claims.by: '0c and the REAL registry was not touched' (the whole real directory listing is compared across a fixture run), '1c every file holds its OWN agent, never a neighbour's', and '1e no temp file was left behind'

claims.claim: ONE FILE PER AGENT, NOT ONE FILE WITH SECTIONS ... the two writes cannot interact at the filesystem level at all.
claims.by: the measured pair -- '1a every agent has a file -- NOT ONE WRITE WAS LOST' against '2a the SHARED-FILE design loses writes under the same concurrency' and '2b ...while the per-agent design lost NONE, on the same machine, in the same run'
claims.note: THIS IS THE CLAIM EVERYTHING ELSE RESTS ON AND IT IS THE ONE AN ARM CANNOT TEST ALONE. Six writers all surviving passes on any design that happens not to race during one run. So section 2 implements the REJECTED design and drives the same concurrency at it: 5 of 6 agents lost their section. The sleep in that writer WIDENS a real read-modify-write window rather than inventing one, and the arm says so in its own output.

claims.claim: WRITES ARE ATOMIC, SO A READER NEVER SEES HALF A FILE.
claims.by: '4b NOT ONE read was torn or half-written -- which is what os.replace() buys and the only thing it buys', guarded by '4a the reader really got to read DURING the writes, so nothing below is passing on zero attempts', plus '3a the file still parses after four processes raced on it'
claims.note: Sabotage-confirmed: replacing the temp+os.replace with a direct write to the final path turns 3a, 3b, 4b and 4d red. The arm measures roughly 1,500 reads taken WHILE four agents write.

claims.claim: Exit 0 clean, 1 a finding, 2 COULD NOT TELL -- never folded into either of the other two.
claims.by: '6a an ABSENT registry is exit 2', '6c an EMPTY registry is exit 2, NOT a clean all-clear', '5c and the run is COULD NOT TELL (2), not a clean registry', and the other direction '5d CONTROL: a registry with no corrupt entry exits 0'

claims.claim: A single unreadable file is an entry with `unreadable` set -- NAMED, never dropped.
claims.by: '5a the corrupt entry is reported UNREADABLE and named' and '5b the healthy entry is STILL reported beside it'
claims.note: Sabotage-confirmed: dropping the unreadable entry instead of naming it turns 5a and 5c red.

claims.claim: LIVENESS IS IMPORTED, NEVER REIMPLEMENTED ... a pid alone is not identity, because a dead session's pid can be reissued.
claims.by: '11a a status from a process that does not exist is NOT reported LIVE' and '11b ...and the row is still shown, with the reason'
claims.note: The import itself is the stronger evidence and it is structural rather than an arm: session_lock_check.owner_state() is called, not copied, so the recycled-pid defence has one implementation on this platform and not two.

claims.claim: It cannot tell whether two agents' task strings describe the SAME WORK -- candidates, not a verdict.
claims.by: '10a two agents on the same subject are named as candidates', the other direction '10b an unrelated third is NOT paired with either', '10d an IDLE agent raises no overlap candidate', and '10c and the report refuses to call a candidate a verdict'

claims.claim: The overlap rule is fixture-checked BEFORE anything is classified -- a rule that has stopped working must refuse, not report a quiet platform.
claims.by: '9b an overlap rule that finds NOTHING exits COULD NOT RUN (2), not 0' and '9c ...and names the rule rather than printing a report', guarded by '9a the teeth anchor is present'

claims.claim: The SessionStart hook FAILS OPEN: a session must start whatever went wrong in here.
claims.by: the four '12 ...: the hook exits 0' arms across a populated, absent, empty and corrupt registry, plus '12 a registry path that is a FILE, not a directory, still exits 0'
claims.note: Failing open is the OPPOSITE of the fail-closed rule this repo applies to checks, and the difference is the consequence rather than an inconsistency: a check that cannot run must not report a pass; an advisory that cannot run must not stop the work. The paired arms pin that failing open is not failing SILENT -- an absent or empty registry still emits the sentence saying the answer is unknown.

claims.claim: It cannot see an agent that never writes a status.
claims.by: no arm
claims.note: A statement about what is absent from the input. There is nothing to drive: it would require an agent that exists and is shown not to appear, which is the definition of the gap rather than a behaviour. The nearest real arm is 6c/6d, which pin that an EMPTY registry is reported as unknown rather than as nobody-working -- the consequence of this limit, which is testable, and is.

claims.claim: It is machine-local: ~/SAIRN-SESSION-LOCKS is not shared between machines.
claims.by: no arm
claims.note: A scope statement about deployment, not behaviour. Testing it would mean asserting the absence of a second machine. Recorded so the limit is in the record rather than only in prose -- it is the same limit the session lock files already have, and it means this registry answers for ONE workstation.

inspections.author_note: SELF-INSPECTION, AND IT IS THE WEAKEST KIND OF EVIDENCE IN THIS FILE. I wrote the tool, I wrote the control, and I read the two against each other -- so the claim-to-arm mapping is the author reading his own header, which is exactly the blind spot the independent-review rule exists for. Recorded because the artefact arrived UNOWNED: nobody had logged an inspection, and an uninspected artefact under the item 47 requirement date is worse than a self-inspected one that says so plainly. IT FOUND ONE REAL DEFECT, IN THE DRAWING RATHER THAN THE BEHAVIOUR: the header's WHAT THIS CAN AND CANNOT SAY section still described v1, which keyed on ATTRIBUTION -- and after the rewrite onto commit SHAPE that paragraph was not stale but BACKWARDS, stating that a commit in which the auditor also edits platform code 'lands in UNATTRIBUTED rather than being caught' when that mixed commit is now the one case the tool refuses. review() carried the correct account three screens below a header that contradicted it; both compile and nothing mechanical could see it. Corrected in the same change with the superseded sentence quoted in place. THREE CLAIMS ARE CARRIED BY NO ARM and are named in the report: the server-side claim cannot be tested from this file and the workflow is currently REPORTING-ONLY after a required-status-check attempt deadlocked direct pushes to main; the hover.json measurement is a hand-reading nothing re-takes; and the build-agent-reaching-in case is synthetic only. It should be re-read by another session -- a control written by the person who chose the design is the least likely place for that design to be doubted.

Without it, the one convention that could break the tool's circularity -- the auditor taking claims so it becomes identifiable -- could not be adopted without first changing the gate. A rule that forbids its own fix is worse than the gap.

The FAI named that as a gap -- the case existed only as a constructed commit dict in --fixtures -- and the arm was added to the end-to-end probe in the same change, building the commit in real git the way the auditor case already was. The second arm matters: it requires the refusal to name the platform path and NOT the claim file, so the bookkeeping carve-out is proved to still hold while the commit is being refused for another reason.

claims.claim: It runs on GitHub's side of the push, where a local hook cannot be switched off.
claims.by: no arm -- this is a property of .github/workflows/hover-separation.yml and the repository's branch rules, not of this file, and nothing this file can execute settles it

The workflow is REPORTING-ONLY: making it a required status check on 2026-09-16 deadlocked direct pushes to main for every clone, because GitHub evaluates required checks before accepting a push while the workflow only runs after one.
